courses.title: What is HTML?
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to make a folder and a file in the terminal with `mkdir` and `touch`, and open a folder in VS Code with `code .` **HTML** is the language used to build every web page in the world. When you open any website, your browser is quietly reading HTML behind the scenes and turning it into the page you see. Do not worry about memorising anything today. We will build a real page together at the end of this lesson. ## HTML is made of tags An HTML page is built out of **tags**. A tag is a keyword wrapped in angle brackets, like this: `

`. Most tags come in a **pair** — an **opening** tag and a **closing** tag. The closing tag looks the same but has a slash `/` in front of the word: ```html

Hello world

``` Read that from left to right: *start a paragraph* (`

`), the text is *Hello world*, *end the paragraph* (`

`). The two tags wrap around the content like a box around it. Here `

` means **paragraph**. There are many other tags — `

` for a big heading, `` for a picture, and more. You will meet them one lesson at a time, so there is no rush. ## Tag, element, content — three words you will hear constantly People use these three words as if everyone already knows them, so here they are plainly: - A **tag** is one of the things in angle brackets: `

` is a tag, and so is `

`. - The **content** is what sits between them: *Hello world*. - An **element** is the whole thing together — opening tag, content, closing tag. ```html

Hello world

``` That whole line is **one element**. It is built from two **tags** with some **content** in between. So when a later lesson says *"give the element a class"* or *"select an element"*, it means the whole thing — not just the `

` part. Tag and element get used loosely in the wild, and now you know why. ## Some tags carry extra information Sometimes a tag needs to know more than just its text. That extra information goes **inside the opening tag** and is called an **attribute**. For example, a link needs to know *where* it should take you: ```html Click me ``` Here `` is a link, `href="https://example.com"` is the attribute that says where the link goes, and *Click me* is the text a person actually clicks. Do not worry about links yet — there is a whole lesson on them later. This is just to show you what an attribute looks like. ## Let us build your first page together This is a **practice page**, just for trying things out — it is not the assignment. Your assignments work differently: each one arrives as its own folder with `index.html`, `style.css` and `script.js` already made for you, and you open those and edit them. Here you are making a file from nothing, once, so you can see where a web page actually comes from. Follow along, step by step. ### Step 1 — Open the terminal in your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen (**File Explorer**). 2. Click **Documents**, then double-click **`lacefi-academy`**. 3. **Right-click** on empty white space inside it → **Show more options** → **Open Git Bash here**. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* ### Step 2 — Make a practice folder and a file Type these three lines, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash mkdir mypage cd mypage touch index.html ``` You just made a folder called `mypage` inside your course folder, stepped into it, and made an empty file called `index.html`. (`index.html` is a special name — it is the file a browser looks for first.) This `mypage` folder is yours to play in. Nothing here is graded, and you can delete it whenever you like. ### Step 3 — Open it in VS Code ```bash code . ``` VS Code opens. Down the left-hand side you will see your file. **Click once on `index.html`** to open it in the big area on the right. ### Step 4 — Type some HTML Type this into the file, then **save it: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. ```html

My first web page

Hi, I made this all by myself!

``` `

` is a big heading. `

` is a paragraph. That is a complete little page. ### Step 5 — See it in your browser 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list on the left. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. **Double-click `index.html`**. It opens in your web browser, and you see your heading and your paragraph on the screen. **This is the loop you will repeat for the rest of the course:** change the file in VS Code → press **Ctrl + S** to save → click back to the browser → press **Ctrl + R** to reload → look at what changed. Try it now: change the words in your `

`, save, reload, and watch the page follow you. **You just built a web page.** Everything from here is simply learning more tags to put inside it. Do the small task below to practise, then move on to the next lesson. ## Recap — the short version - Most tags come in a pair, and the closing one carries a slash: `

` opens it, `

` closes it. A forgotten slash is the most common first mistake. - A **tag** is the part in angle brackets, the **content** is what sits between the tags, and the **element** is all of it together. - An **attribute** goes inside the opening tag and gives it extra information, like `href="https://example.com"` on a link. - `index.html` is a special file name — it is the one a browser looks for first. - The loop never changes: edit the file, **Ctrl + S** to save, click back to the browser, **Ctrl + R** to reload.

Click `index.html` in VS Code, type an `

` heading and a `

` paragraph, and save with **Ctrl + S**
Right-click `index.html` → **Reveal in File Explorer**, double-click it, then change a word, save, and press **Ctrl + R**
Push your work, then submit with a tag

courses.title: The shape of every page
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write a heading and a paragraph in an `index.html` file and open that file in your browser Every real web page starts from the same little skeleton. Copy it, then fill in the middle. Here it is: ```html My Page

Hello

``` What each part means, in plain words: - `` — tells the browser *this is a modern web page*. Always the first line. - `` — wraps the whole page. `lang="en"` just says the page is in English. - `` — information **about** the page that visitors do not see: the character set, screen settings, and the `` (the name shown on the browser tab). - `<body>` — everything people actually **see**: your headings, text, images, and so on. From now on, put your work inside the `<body>`. ## Where you will see this happen Most of this skeleton is invisible on the page, so it can look as though nothing happened. The `<title>` is the part you can actually check. 1. Save the file with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: **Command + S**)*. 2. **Right-click `index.html`** in VS Code's file list → **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. **Double-click** `index.html` to open it in your browser. 4. Look at the **tab** at the very top of the browser window, not at the page. The words you put inside `<title>` are printed there. The `<body>` is the only part that shows on the page itself. Change the `<title>`, press **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** — the tab name follows you. ## Recap — the short version - `<!doctype html>` is always the very first line, with nothing above it. - Everything a visitor sees goes inside `<body>`. The `<head>` holds information **about** the page, so nothing you put there appears on the page. - The `<title>` shows on the browser **tab**, not on the page. - The skeleton nests: `<html>` wraps `<head>` and `<body>`, and each of them needs its closing tag.

Change the `<title>` to your own page name
Put an `<h1>` heading inside the `<body>`, save with **Ctrl + S**, and open the file in your browser
Push your work, then submit with a tag

Two tags do the heavy lifting: headings and paragraphs. **Real example:** open any news story on `https://www.bbc.com/news`. Notice the big **headline** at the top, the smaller **section titles**, and the **paragraphs** of the story. That is exactly what you are about to build. ## Headings Headings are titles. There are six sizes, from `

` (biggest) down to `

` (smallest). Use **one** `

` for the main title of the page, then `

My Cooking Blog

Breakfast

Dinner

``` Do not pick a heading just because of its size — pick it for its **meaning** (main title, then section, then sub-section). This is how screen readers and Google understand your page. ## Paragraphs A paragraph is a block of normal text, wrapped in `

`: ```html

This is my first paragraph.

And this is a second one.

``` ## Making words stand out - `` marks text as **important** (browsers show it bold). - `` adds **emphasis** (browsers show it in italics). ```html

This is really important and a little exciting.

``` **Try it:** on your page, add an `

` with your name, an `

` called *About me*, and a paragraph under it. Make one word ``. ## Recap — the short version - Use one `

` for the page, then `

` for its sections. Pick a heading for its meaning, not because you like its size. - There are six heading levels, `

` down to `

`, and `

` is the biggest. - `` marks text as important and shows bold; `` adds emphasis and shows italic. Both need a closing tag. - Every paragraph needs its own `

` element. Pressing Enter twice in the file does not make a new paragraph.

courses.title: Links
courses.description: > **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write headings and paragraphs, and mark a word as important with `` Links are what turn a pile of separate pages into a **web**. Every time you click a word and jump somewhere new, that is a link doing its job. **Real example:** open Wikipedia at `https://en.wikipedia.org` and click any blue word inside an article. Every single one is a link. That is the whole idea of the web in one page — go try it. ## Making a link You make a link with the `` tag (the *a* stands for *anchor*) and its `href` attribute — the address it points to: ```html Go to Wikipedia ``` The words between the tags (*Go to Wikipedia*) are what a person clicks. The `href` is where they land. ## Three links you will use all the time - **To another website** — use the full address: ```html Google ``` - **To another page in your own project** — just the file name: ```html About me ``` - **To open in a new tab** — add `target="_blank"`: ```html Open Google in a new tab ``` **Try it:** add a link to your favourite website on your page, save, and click it in your browser. Then make a second link that opens in a new tab. ## Recap — the short version - The address goes in the `href` attribute inside the opening tag. The words people click go between `` and ``. - A link to another website needs the full address including `https://`. Leave it off and the browser hunts for a file in your own folder instead. - A link to one of your own pages needs only the file name, like `about.html`. - `target="_blank"` makes the link open in a new tab.

courses.description: > **Before this lesson,** you should be able to add a link with `` and point its `href` at a web address A page of only text is dull. Images bring it to life. **Real example:** open Unsplash at `https://unsplash.com` — it is a giant wall of photos, and every one is an HTML image. You can even grab a free photo there to use on your own page later. ## Adding an image Use the `` tag. It is a lonely tag — no closing partner needed: ```html ``` Two attributes matter: - `src` — the **source**: where the picture is. This can be a file on your computer (`cat.jpg`) or a full web address (`https://.../cat.jpg`). - `alt` — the **alternative text**: a short description of the picture in words. It is read aloud to people who cannot see the image, and it shows if the picture fails to load. **Always** write a clear, honest alt. Good alt: `alt="A red bicycle leaning on a brick wall"`. Lazy alt: `alt="image"` (do not do this). ## Adding a caption Wrap the image and a caption together: ```html ``` **Try it:** download a photo from `https://unsplash.com`, save it next to your `index.html`, and show it on your page with a clear `alt`. ## Recap — the short version - `` has no closing tag. It is written on its own: ``. - `src` is where the picture is. A plain file name means *next to my `index.html`*, so the photo has to sit in the same folder. - `alt` is a short honest description. It is read aloud to people who cannot see the picture, and it shows if the picture fails to load. - `

Scroll it and notice the bold header row at the top. ## Building a table, row by row - `` wraps the whole thing. - `` is one **row** (*table row*). - ``, and every `` sits inside the `

Name Age

courses.title: Meet the terminal
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to install VS Code and open Git Bash on Windows, or Terminal on a Mac

The **terminal** is simply a window where you talk to your computer by **typing** instead of clicking. That is all it is. You type one short instruction, press **Enter**, and the computer does it.

It looks plain and a little scary the first time. That is completely normal. You will only ever need about five commands, and you **cannot break your computer** by trying them here. Let us go slowly, one step at a time.

## Step 1 — Make one folder for the whole course

Everything you build in this course will live in **one folder** on your computer, so your work stays tidy and easy to find. Let us make it now.

1. Open **File Explorer** (the yellow folder icon on your taskbar).
2. On the left, click **Documents**.
3. Right-click on an empty white space → **New** → **Folder**.
4. Name the new folder **`lacefi-academy`** and press **Enter**.

That is it. From now on, **every assignment you clone goes inside `Documents\lacefi-academy`**. (On a Mac it is the same: make a `lacefi-academy` folder inside your Documents.)

## Step 2 — Open the terminal *inside* that folder

Here is the easiest way to open the terminal already pointing at your folder — do it this way and you will avoid a lot of confusion.

**On Windows:**

1. Open your **`Documents\lacefi-academy`** folder in File Explorer.
2. **Right-click** on an empty white space inside the folder.
3. Click **Show more options** (on Windows 11), then click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with some text and a **blinking cursor** — and it is already inside your `lacefi-academy` folder. (That blinking cursor is the computer waiting for you to type.)

*(If you don't see "Open Git Bash here", you may not have installed Git Bash yet — go back to the "Set up your computer" lesson.)*

**On Mac:** open the **Terminal** app (press **Command + Space**, type *Terminal*, press Enter), then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press Enter to move into your folder.

## Step 3 — What you are looking at

The line with the blinking cursor is called the **prompt** — the computer quietly saying *I am ready, tell me what to do.* You type a command there, press **Enter**, and it runs. You barely touch the mouse in here — just type, then Enter.

## Step 4 — Where am I? (`pwd`)

Type this exactly, then press **Enter**:

```bash
pwd
```

`pwd` means *print working directory*. It shows the folder you are in right now — you should see it ends with `lacefi-academy`. That is *where am I?* answered.

## Step 5 — What is here? (`ls`)

```bash
ls
```

`ls` means *list*. It shows the files and folders where you are — like opening a drawer to see what is inside. (Your folder is empty for now, so you may see nothing. That is fine.)

## Step 6 — Move around (`cd`)

`cd` means *change directory* (directory is just another word for folder). To go **into** a folder, type `cd` then its name:

```bash
cd practice
```

To go **back out** one step:

```bash
cd ..
```

The two dots mean *the folder just above this one*.

## Step 7 — Make a folder (`mkdir`)

```bash
mkdir practice
```

`mkdir` means *make directory*. Type `ls` again and your new `practice` folder appears.

## Step 8 — Make a file (`touch`)

```bash
touch notes.txt
```

`touch` makes a new empty file. You now know how to make folders and files from the keyboard.

## Step 9 — Open the folder in VS Code (`code .`)

When you want to write code in the folder you are in, type:

```bash
code .
```

The dot means *this folder, the one I am in now*. VS Code opens, ready to edit.

## That is it — your whole toolkit

- `pwd` — where am I?
- `ls` — what is here?
- `cd name` — go into a folder. `cd ..` — go back out.
- `mkdir name` — make a folder.
- `touch name` — make a file.
- `code .` — open this folder in VS Code.

**Remember the big habit:** open your `lacefi-academy` folder, right-click, **Open Git Bash here** — and you're ready to work. You'll do this at the start of every assignment.

**Try it:** open Git Bash inside your `lacefi-academy` folder, run `pwd`, then `mkdir practice`, then `cd practice`, then `ls`. Go slowly — you cannot break anything.

## Recap — the short version

- `cd ..` — two dots — takes you back **out** one folder. `cd name` takes you **into** one.
- The dot in `code .` means *this folder, the one I am in right now*.
- `pwd` says where you are, `ls` says what is here, `mkdir` makes a folder and `touch` makes a file.
- Opening the terminal by right-clicking inside a folder means it already points at that folder, which avoids most early confusion.
- A command only runs when you press **Enter**, and nothing you type in here can break your computer.

Run `pwd`, then `mkdir practice`, then `cd practice`, then `ls`, pressing **Enter** after each
Type `code .` to open the folder you are standing in inside VS Code

courses.title: Boxes: div and span
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to build a page with headings, paragraphs, links, images and lists Sometimes you need to **group** things together — a card, a section, a menu bar. HTML gives you two plain "boxes" for that: `
` and ``. **Real example:** open a site like `https://www.airbnb.com`, right-click any listing card, and choose **Inspect**. You will see it is made of many `
` boxes nested inside each other. Divs are the building blocks of nearly every layout on the web. ## First, a tool worth knowing: Inspect Several lessons — including this one — ask you to *right-click something and choose Inspect*. Here is what that does, in case you have never done it. Every website you visit is built from HTML sitting on someone else's computer, and your browser will happily show it to you. courses.title: What is CSS?
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write an HTML page and add tags inside its `<head>`

HTML builds the **structure** of a page. **CSS** makes it **beautiful** — colours, fonts, spacing, layout. If HTML is the skeleton, CSS is the skin, hair, and clothes.

**Real example:** open `https://www.csszengarden.com`. Every design on that page uses the *exact same HTML* — only the CSS changes. That is the power of CSS: same bones, endless looks.

## How to add CSS

The tidy way is a separate file. Make a file called `style.css` next to your `index.html`, then link it inside the `<head>` of your HTML:

```html
<head>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
</head>
```

Now anything you write in `style.css` styles your page.

## A CSS rule

CSS is made of **rules**. Each rule picks something and gives it a look:

```css
h1 {
  color: blue;
  font-size: 40px;
}
```

Read it as: *find every `<h1>`, and make its text blue and 40 pixels big.*

- `h1` is the **selector** — what to style.
- `color` and `font-size` are **properties** — what to change.
- `blue` and `40px` are the **values**.
- The curly braces `{ }` hold the rules, and every line ends with a semicolon `;`.

**Try it:** make a `style.css`, link it from your HTML, and turn your `<h1>` a colour you like.

## Where you will see this happen

1. Save both files with **Ctrl + S**.
2. **Right-click `index.html`** in VS Code → **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)* → **double-click** it.
3. Your `<h1>` should now be the colour you chose. Nothing else on the page changes, so this one heading is the whole proof.
4. If the heading is still plain black, the stylesheet is not linked. Open `index.html` and check that `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` sits inside `<head>`, spelled exactly, and that your file really is called `style.css`.
5. After every edit: save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R**.

## Recap — the short version

- CSS in `style.css` does nothing at all until `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` sits inside the `<head>` of your HTML — a typo in that file name leaves the page completely unstyled.
- A rule has the shape `selector { property: value; }`: the selector picks what to style, and everything you want to change goes inside the curly braces `{ }`.
- A colon `:` sits between the property and the value, and a semicolon `;` ends every declaration.
- CSS uses American spelling: the property is `color`, never `colour`, and the browser quietly ignores a property name it does not recognise.
- Same HTML with different CSS gives a completely different-looking page — that is what `csszengarden.com` demonstrates.

**Real example:** open `https://coolors.co` and press the spacebar to generate a colour palette. Those are exactly the kinds of colours you can drop into CSS.

## Two colour properties

- `color` — the colour of **text**.
- `background-color` — the colour **behind** an element.

```css
body {
  background-color: #f5f5f5;
}
h1 {
  color: crimson;
}
```

## Ways to write a colour

- **Names:** `red`, `blue`, `crimson`, `teal` (about 140 names exist).
- **Hex codes:** `#ff0000` is red, `#00b894` is green. They start with `#` and let you pick *any* colour. You copy these straight from a site like Coolors.

**Try it:** give your whole page a soft `background-color` on the `body`, and make your `<h1>` a bold `color`.

## Recap — the short version

- `color` sets the colour of the text, and `background-color` sets the colour behind the element — swapping the two is the usual reason a box comes out the wrong colour.
- Both are spelled the American way. `colour` is not a CSS property, and a misspelt property is ignored without any warning.
- A hex code starts with a hash, like `#00b894`; a colour name like `crimson` takes no hash.
- Set the page background on `body` so it covers the whole page rather than one box.
- A palette site such as `coolors.co` gives you hex codes you can paste straight into your CSS.

Good-looking text makes a page easy and pleasant to read.

**Real example:** notice how articles on `https://medium.com` use a clean, large, well-spaced font with lots of breathing room. That is all CSS.

## The main text properties

```css
p {
  font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
  font-size: 18px;
  font-weight: bold;
  text-align: center;
  color: #333;
}
```

- `font-family` — which font to use. List a backup, ending in `sans-serif` (plain) or `serif` (with little feet).
- `font-size` — how big, e.g. `18px`.
- `font-weight` — `normal` or `bold`.
- `text-align` — `left`, `center`, or `right`.
- `color` — the text colour.

A comfy trick for readable body text: `font-size: 18px` and a dark grey like `#333` instead of pure black.

**Try it:** set a nice `font-family` on your `body`, make paragraphs `18px`, and centre your `<h1>` with `text-align`.

## Recap — the short version

- `text-align: center` is spelled the American way — `centre` does nothing at all, and the browser gives you no warning.
- `color` sets the colour of the text, and it is the American spelling here too.
- `font-family` takes a list, and the browser uses the first font it actually has, so end the list with `sans-serif` or `serif`.
- `text-align` moves text inside its own box, so the box has to be wider than the text for the change to show.
- Body text at `18px` in a dark grey such as `#333` is more comfortable to read than small pure-black text.

Here is the secret to spacing and layout: **every element on a page is a box.** Once you see the box, you can control the space everywhere.

**Real example:** on any website, right-click something and choose **Inspect**, then hover over the element. You will see a coloured diagram — blue content, green padding, orange margin. That is the box model.

## The four parts, from inside out

- **content** — the text or image itself.
- **padding** — space *inside* the box, between the content and the border.
- **border** — a line drawn around the box.
- **margin** — space *outside* the box, pushing other things away.

```css
.card {
  width: 300px;
  padding: 20px;
  border: 2px solid gray;
  margin: 16px;
}
```

Think of a framed photo on a wall: the photo is the **content**, the white mount around it is the **padding**, the wooden frame is the **border**, and the gap to the next frame is the **margin**.

**Try it:** put a `border`, some `padding`, and a `margin` on a `<div>` in your page and watch the space appear around it.

## Recap — the short version

- Padding is the space **inside** the border and margin is the space **outside** it — that one distinction explains most spacing problems you will hit.
- Every element on a page is a box with four parts, from the inside out: content, padding, border, margin.
- Right-click an element and choose **Inspect** to see the box drawn in colour: blue content, green padding, orange margin.
- `border: 2px solid gray;` gives the width, the style and the colour in one go, in that order.
- Picture a framed photo: the photo is the content, the mount is the padding, the frame is the border, and the gap to the next frame is the margin.

courses.title: Variables: const and let
courses.description:
A **variable** is a named box that holds a value, so you can use it by name and change it later.

## Making a variable

```javascript
const name = "Ada";
let score = 10;
```

- `const` — a box whose value **never changes**. Use this most of the time.
- `let` — a box whose value **can change** later.

The `=` means *put the value on the right into the box on the left*. It is not 'equals' like in maths.

## Using and changing them

```javascript
const greeting = "Hello";
const name = "Ada";
console.log(greeting + ", " + name + "!");   // Hello, Ada!

let score = 10;
score = score + 5;        // only works because score is `let`
console.log(score);       // 15
```

The `+` between two strings **joins** them together (that is called concatenation). Between two numbers it adds.

Try changing a `const` after setting it and you will get an error — that is `const` doing its job.

courses.title: Writing functions
courses.description:
A **function** is a named piece of code that takes some input, does a job, and gives back a result. It is the single most important idea in programming, and from here on you will write one in almost every assignment.

## Writing one

```javascript
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
```

- `function` starts it, `double` is its name.
- `n` is a **parameter**: the input, named so you can use it inside.
- `return` hands a value back to whoever called the function.

## Calling one

```javascript
console.log(double(5));   // 10
console.log(double(21));  // 42
```

You give it different inputs and it gives back different results. That is the power: write the logic once, use it many times.

## Guarding against bad input

What if someone calls your function with nothing, or with `null`? Good code checks first:

```javascript
function greet(name) {
  if (!name) {
    return "Hello, friend!";   // no name given
  }
  return "Hello, " + name + "!";
}
```

`if (!name)` means *if name is empty, null, or undefined*. This **guard** is why `greet(null)` gives a sensible answer instead of `Hello, null!`. From now on your assignments will test these edge cases on purpose, so always guard your inputs.

## Letting the checker see your function

So the autograder can call your function, add this as the **last line** of `app.js`, naming each function you wrote:

```javascript
module.exports = { greet };
```

That is it. Write the function, export it, and the checker runs it against several inputs — including tricky ones like empty text and `null`.

courses.title: Events: reacting to clicks
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to change an element's text, style or classes from `script.js`

An **event** is something that happens on the page — a click, a key press, a mouse hover, a form submit. JavaScript can **listen** for an event and run code when it happens. This is what makes a page truly interactive: it *reacts* to the person using it.

## Listen for a click

Start with a button:

```html
<button id="myButton">Click me</button>
```

Then in `script.js`, select it and attach a listener:

```javascript
const button = document.querySelector("#myButton");

button.addEventListener("click", function () {
  console.log("You clicked me!");
});
```

Read it as: *"On the button, listen for a **click**; when it happens, run this function."* Click the button and watch the console.

The function you pass in only runs **later**, each time the event fires. This is a big shift from top-to-bottom code: you're setting up a *reaction* and waiting.

## Make the click change the page

Combine events with the DOM changes you just learned:

```javascript
const button = document.querySelector("#myButton");
const title  = document.querySelector("#title");

button.addEventListener("click", function () {
  title.textContent = "You clicked!";
  title.style.color = "green";
});
```

Now clicking the button rewrites and recolours the heading. That's a real, interactive web page — built from pieces you already know.

## Other common events

The pattern is always `element.addEventListener("eventName", function)`. Swap the name:

- `"click"` — a click
- `"mouseover"` / `"mouseout"` — pointer enters / leaves
- `"keydown"` — a key is pressed
- `"input"` — the value of a text box changes
- `"submit"` — a form is submitted (next lesson)

## The everyday pattern

1. **Select** the element.
2. **`addEventListener`** with an event name.
3. In the function, **do something** (change the DOM, run a calculation…).

Master this and you can build almost any interaction.

**Try it:** add a button and, when it's clicked, change your heading's text (or colour).

## Recap — the short version

- Hand the function to `addEventListener` **without brackets after it**. Brackets would run it immediately instead of saving it for later.
- The event name is a string in quotes and all lower case: `"click"`, not `"Click"`.
- The code inside the listener runs each time the event happens, which may be long after the rest of your script has finished.
- The pattern never changes: select the element, `addEventListener` with an event name, then change something inside the function.
- Swap the name for a different reaction: `"mouseover"`, `"keydown"`, `"input"`, `"submit"`.

**Syntax** is the set of rules for how code must be written so the computer understands it. JavaScript's rules are gentle. Here are the ones you need now.

## Statements end with a semicolon

Each instruction is a **statement**, and we end it with a semicolon `;`:

```javascript
console.log("first");
console.log("second");
```

## Printing more than one thing

`console.log` can print several values at once if you separate them with commas. It puts a space between them:

```javascript
console.log("2 + 2 =", 2 + 2);   // prints: 2 + 2 = 4
```

Notice something important: `"2 + 2 ="` is in quotes, so it is **text** and prints exactly as written. `2 + 2` has no quotes, so the computer actually **works it out** and prints `4`.

## Text vs. numbers

- Text (called a **string**) goes in quotes: `"hello"`, `"42"`.
- Numbers have no quotes: `42`, `3.5`.

This difference matters a lot, and the next lessons dig into it.

courses.title: Data types

Every value in JavaScript has a **type**. The three you use most as a beginner:

- **string** — text, in quotes: `"hello"`, `"42"`
- **number** — any number: `42`, `3.5`, `-7`
- **boolean** — `true` or `false`, the answer to a yes/no question

## Checking a type

`typeof` tells you the type of a value:

```javascript
console.log(typeof "hello");  // string
console.log(typeof 42);       // number
console.log(typeof true);     // boolean
```

## Why the type matters

`"42"` (a string) and `42` (a number) look alike but behave differently:

```javascript
console.log("42" + 1);  // 421  (joined as text!)
console.log(42 + 1);    // 43   (added as numbers)
```

That surprise — text pretending to be a number — causes many beginner bugs. The next lesson shows how to convert between types on purpose.

courses.title: Operators
courses.description:
**Operators** are the symbols that do work on values.

## Maths operators

```javascript
console.log(7 + 6);   // 13
console.log(7 - 6);   // 1
console.log(7 * 6);   // 42
console.log(7 / 2);   // 3.5
console.log(7 % 2);   // 1   (remainder: what is left after dividing)
```

`%` (called **modulo**) gives the remainder. `7 % 2` is `1` because 7 divided by 2 is 3 with 1 left over. It is how you check if a number is even (`n % 2 === 0`).

## Comparison operators

These ask a yes/no question and give back a boolean:

```javascript
console.log(5 > 3);    // true
console.log(5 < 3);    // false
console.log(5 === 5);  // true   (=== means 'exactly equal')
console.log(5 !== 3);  // true   (!== means 'not equal')
```

Always compare with **`===`** (three equals), not `=`. One `=` *assigns* a value; three `===` *compares*. You will lean on these constantly once you start making decisions.

courses.title: Type conversion

## Text to number, number to text

```javascript
Number("5")    // 5    (string -> number)
String(5)      // "5"  (number -> string)
```

This matters because text and numbers behave differently with `+`:

```javascript
console.log("5" + 2);           // "52"  (joined as text)
console.log(Number("5") + 2);    // 7     (added as numbers)
```

When a number arrives as text (for example, typed by a user), wrap it in `Number(...)` before doing maths.

## Truthy and falsy

Any value can be read as a yes/no (boolean). These count as **false** ("falsy"): `false`, `0`, `""` (empty text), `null`, and `undefined`. Almost everything else is **true** ("truthy").

```javascript
Boolean("")      // false  (empty text)
Boolean("hi")    // true
Boolean(0)       // false
```

This becomes very useful soon: it is how you check *'did I actually get a value?'* — the start of writing safe code.

courses.description:
`Math` is a built in object full of useful number helpers. A few:

```javascript
console.log(Math.max(3, 7, 2)); // 7
console.log(Math.min(3, 7, 2)); // 2
console.log(Math.round(4.6));   // 5
console.log(Math.abs(-9));      // 9
```

`Math.max` wants its numbers as separate arguments, not a single array. The **spread** `...` turns an array into separate arguments:

courses.description:
Every programmer writes bugs. Debugging is the skill of finding them calmly.

Three habits that find most bugs fast:

- **Read the error and its line number.** The message usually names what went wrong and where. Start there.
- **Print what your code actually believes.** `console.log(arr.length)` shows you the real value, which is often not what you assumed.
- **Check your assumptions one by one.** The bug is almost always a gap between what you think is true and what is true.

### A classic: the off by one

Array indexes start at `0`, so an array of length `3` has its last item at index `2`, which is `arr.length - 1`. Writing `arr[arr.length]` reaches past the end and gives `undefined`. When a test expected a value but got `undefined`, suspect an off by one first.

courses.description:
A **regular expression** (regex) describes a pattern of text. You can test whether a string matches a pattern:

```javascript
let pattern = /^0\d{9}$/;
console.log(pattern.test('0712345678')); // true
console.log(pattern.test('123'));         // false
```

Reading `/^0\d{9}$/` piece by piece:

- `^` means the start of the text
- `0` means a literal zero
- `\d` means any digit, and `{9}` means exactly nine of them
- `$` means the end of the text

So the whole pattern says: a zero, then nine digits, and nothing else. `.test(text)` returns `true` or `false`.

### Guard first

`.test()` quietly converts a non string to text first, so `pattern.test(null)` returns `false` rather than throwing. If you need to treat non text as invalid, check `typeof text === 'string'` yourself.

Some work takes time: waiting for a timer, reading a file, talking to a server. JavaScript does not stop and freeze while it waits. Instead, such work returns a **Promise**, a value that arrives later.

An `async` function lets you work with promises as if they were ordinary values, using `await` to pause until the value is ready:

```javascript
async function greetLater(name) {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 5)); // wait 5ms
  return 'Hi, ' + name + '!';
}
```

- An `async` function always returns a Promise.
- `await` pauses inside the function until the thing you are waiting on finishes, then gives you its value.
- To read the result from outside, you use `.then(value => ...)`, or `await` it inside another `async` function.

The guards you already know still apply: check the input before you trust it.

courses.title: CSS syntax
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to link a `style.css` file from your HTML and write a rule that styles a whole tag such as `h1`

Every line of CSS follows the same simple shape. Once you can read that shape, all of CSS is just learning new words to put in it.

## A CSS rule

Here is one **rule**:

```css
h1 {
  color: blue;
  font-size: 40px;
}
```

Three parts to name:

- **Selector** — `h1`. *Which* elements to style (here, every `<h1>`).
- **Property** — `color`, `font-size`. *What* you want to change.
- **Value** — `blue`, `40px`. *How* you want it.

A property and its value together (`color: blue;`) are called a **declaration**. You can have as many declarations as you like inside the `{ }`.

## The punctuation matters

- A **colon** `:` sits between the property and the value.
- A **semicolon** `;` ends each declaration. Forgetting it is the #1 beginner CSS bug — the next line silently stops working.
- **Curly braces** `{ }` wrap all the declarations for a selector.

```css
p {
  color: gray;      /* colon after property, semicolon at the end */
  line-height: 1.6;
}
```

## Comments

Notes for humans, ignored by the browser. CSS comments look like this:

```css
/* This styles the main heading */
h1 {
  color: crimson;
}
```

(Note: `//` is NOT a comment in CSS — only `/* ... */` works.)

## Whitespace is free

Spaces, tabs and new lines don't matter to the browser, so lay your CSS out to be readable — one declaration per line, indented inside the braces. Your future self will thank you.

**Try it:** in a `style.css`, write a rule that selects `body` and sets a `color` and a `font-size`, each ending in a semicolon.

## Recap — the short version

- A missing semicolon `;` is the commonest CSS bug — the declaration after it silently stops working, so check your punctuation before you doubt anything else.
- The shape never changes: `selector { property: value; }`. Colon between property and value, semicolon at the end of each declaration, braces around the lot.
- A property and its value together are one **declaration**, and you can put as many declarations as you like inside one set of braces.
- A CSS comment is written `/* like this */`. `//` is not a comment in CSS and will break the rule it sits in.
- Properties use American spelling — `color`, not `colour` — and spaces, tabs and new lines make no difference to the browser, so lay your rules out to be readable.

courses.title: Padding and margin
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to name the four parts of the box model and put a border on an element

Good spacing is what separates a page that looks "designed" from one that looks cramped. In CSS, spacing comes from two properties: **padding** and **margin**. Getting these two straight is one of the most useful things you can learn.

## The difference

Picture a framed photo on a wall:

- **Padding** is the space *inside* the frame, between the photo and the frame edge — space **inside** an element, between its content and its border.
- **Margin** is the space *outside* the frame, between this frame and the next — space **outside** an element, pushing other things away.

```css
.card {
  padding: 20px;   /* space inside the card */
  margin: 16px;    /* space around the card */
}
```

## One value, or four

Give one value and it applies to all four sides. Give more to target specific sides:

```css
padding: 20px;               /* all four sides */
padding: 10px 20px;          /* top+bottom 10, left+right 20 */
padding: 10px 20px 30px 40px;/* top, right, bottom, left (clockwise) */
```

Or set a single side by name:

```css
margin-top: 40px;
margin-bottom: 20px;
padding-left: 12px;
```

## Centering a block with margin

A classic trick: `margin: 0 auto` centers a block that has a width, by splitting the leftover space evenly left and right:

```css
.container {
  max-width: 800px;
  margin: 0 auto;    /* centered on the page */
}
```

## A tip for debugging layout

When spacing looks off, temporarily add `border: 1px solid red;` to an element so you can *see* its box, then adjust its padding and margin. Remove the border when it looks right.

**Try it:** in `style.css`, give a box some `padding` and some `margin`, then center a `.container` with `max-width` and `margin: 0 auto`.

## Recap — the short version

- `margin: 0 auto` only centres a block that has a `width` or a `max-width`. Without one the block is already full width, so nothing appears to happen.
- Padding pushes the content away from the border; margin pushes other elements away from this one.
- Four values run clockwise from the top: `padding: 10px 20px 30px 40px;` is top, right, bottom, left.
- Two values mean top-and-bottom first, then left-and-right: `padding: 10px 20px;`.
- When spacing looks wrong, add `border: 1px solid red;` for a moment so you can see the box, then take it off again.

courses.title: Borders and rounded corners
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to space an element with padding and margin, and centre a container with `margin: 0 auto`

Borders draw a line around an element. They're simple, useful for separating things, and — with rounded corners — a big part of modern-looking design.

## A basic border

The `border` shorthand takes three things: **width**, **style**, and **colour**:

```css
.box {
  border: 2px solid black;
}
```

That's a 2px-wide, solid, black line around the box. The style can be `solid`, `dashed`, `dotted`, `double`, and a few others — `solid` is by far the most common.

## One side at a time

```css
.quote {
  border-left: 4px solid #6a11cb;   /* just a left accent bar */
}
.row {
  border-bottom: 1px solid #ddd;    /* a divider under each row */
}
```

A single `border-bottom` is a clean way to make list dividers or underline a heading.

## Rounded corners

`border-radius` rounds the corners — one of the most-used properties in real design:

```css
.card {
  border: 1px solid #ddd;
  border-radius: 8px;      /* gently rounded */
}
.avatar {
  border-radius: 50%;      /* a perfect circle (on a square image) */
}
```

`border-radius: 50%` turning a square into a circle is the trick behind almost every round profile picture you've seen.

## Outline — a border that takes no space

`outline` looks like a border but sits *outside* the box and doesn't affect layout. You'll mostly meet it as the glow around a focused input — don't remove it without providing another focus style, because keyboard users rely on it.

**Try it:** in `style.css`, give a `.card` a `border` and a `border-radius`, and give another element just a `border-bottom` as a divider.

## Recap — the short version

- `border-radius: 50%` turns a square into a circle — the trick behind almost every round profile picture. The element has to be square for the circle to come out round.
- A border needs all three parts. Leave out the style, as in `border: 2px black;`, and no line is drawn at all.
- The `border` shorthand takes them in order: width, style, colour — `border: 2px solid black;`.
- You can set one side on its own with `border-left`, `border-bottom` and the rest; a single `border-bottom` makes a tidy divider under a row or a heading.
- `outline` looks like a border but sits outside the box and takes up no space. Do not remove the focus outline without replacing it, because keyboard users rely on it.

courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to put a border and rounded corners on a box

By default, elements size themselves — a block stretches full width, a box grows to fit its content. Often you want to take control. That's what `width`, `height`, and their `max`/`min` cousins are for.

## width and height

```css
.box {
  width: 300px;
  height: 200px;
}
```

Simple, but fixed sizes can cause trouble: a `width: 300px` box will overflow a phone screen narrower than 300px. That's where the flexible versions come in.

## max-width — the responsive hero

`max-width` says "*up to* this wide, but shrink if there's less room." This one line is the backbone of pages that work on phones:

```css
.container {
  max-width: 900px;   /* never wider than 900 */
  margin: 0 auto;     /* centered */
}
img {
  max-width: 100%;    /* never wider than its container */
}
```

`img { max-width: 100%; }` is a rule you should put on almost every project — it stops images from blowing out of their box on small screens.

## min-width and min-height

The opposite floor: "at least this big."

```css
.button {
  min-width: 120px;   /* don't get narrower than this, even with short text */
}
```

## The box-sizing fix

By default, if you set `width: 300px` and then add padding and a border, the box becomes *wider* than 300px (padding and border are added on top). This surprises everyone. The fix, which most projects apply once at the top:

```css
* {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
```

Now `width` includes the padding and border — the box is exactly the width you asked for. Add this to the top of your stylesheet and sizing suddenly behaves.

**Try it:** in `style.css`, add `* { box-sizing: border-box; }`, give a `.container` a `max-width` and `margin: 0 auto`, and add `img { max-width: 100%; }`.

## Recap — the short version

- `* { box-sizing: border-box; }` at the top of your stylesheet makes `width` include the padding and the border. Without it, a `width: 300px` box with padding is wider than 300px.
- `max-width` means "up to this wide, but shrink if there is less room", and that one line is what keeps a page usable on a phone.
- `img { max-width: 100%; }` belongs in almost every project — it stops images bursting out of their box on small screens.
- A fixed `width` in pixels will overflow any screen narrower than that number.
- `min-width` sets a floor instead: the element never gets narrower than that, even with very short content.

courses.title: Fonts and typography
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to set `font-family`, `font-size` and `text-align` on the text of a page

Typography — the choice and styling of fonts — has a huge effect on how professional a page feels. A little care here goes a long way.

## Choosing a font-family

`font-family` sets the typeface. You give a **list**, and the browser uses the first one available:

```css
body {
  font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif;
}
```

The last item is a **generic fallback** — always end with one:
- `sans-serif` — clean, no little feet (Arial, Helvetica). Great for screens.
- `serif` — has little feet (Times). More traditional.
- `monospace` — every letter the same width (Courier). For code.

## Font size and weight

```css
h1 {
  font-size: 40px;
  font-weight: bold;    /* or 700 */
}
p {
  font-size: 16px;
  font-weight: normal;  /* or 400 */
}
```

`font-weight` can be words (`normal`, `bold`) or numbers (`100`–`900`, where `400` is normal and `700` is bold).

## Line height — the readability lever

`line-height` sets the space between lines. Body text is much easier to read with a bit of breathing room — around `1.5` to `1.6`:

```css
p {
  line-height: 1.6;
}
```

This single change makes paragraphs feel far less cramped.

## Using a Google Font

Want a nicer font than the ones already on the computer? Google Fonts are free. Add a `<link>` in your HTML `<head>`:

```html
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Poppins&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
```

Then use it in your CSS:

```css
body {
  font-family: "Poppins", sans-serif;
}
```

(Browse the fonts and copy the exact link at fonts.google.com.)

**Try it:** in `style.css`, set a `font-family` (ending in a generic fallback) on `body`, give `h1` a bigger `font-size`, and set `line-height: 1.6` on your paragraphs.

## Recap — the short version

- `line-height: 1.6` on body text is the single biggest readability win, and it takes no unit — write `1.6`, not `1.6px`.
- Always end a `font-family` list with a generic fallback: `sans-serif`, `serif` or `monospace`.
- A font name containing a space goes in quotes: `font-family: "Poppins", sans-serif;`.
- A Google Font needs its `<link>` in the HTML `<head>` as well as the `font-family` in your CSS — the CSS on its own will not fetch the font.
- `font-weight` can be a word or a number: `400` is `normal` and `700` is `bold`.

`float` is an older layout tool. Modern layouts use Flexbox and Grid (coming next), but float still has one everyday use and you'll see it in lots of existing code, so it's worth a short lesson.

## What float does

`float` pushes an element to the left or right and lets text and inline content **wrap around it** — exactly like an image in a magazine article with text flowing around it:

```css
img {
  float: left;
  margin-right: 16px;
}
```

Now the paragraph text wraps neatly to the right of the image. That "text wrapping around an image" effect is float's best, still-useful job today.

## Clearing a float

Floated elements are taken out of the normal flow, which can make their container collapse (shrink to nothing) or make later content slide up beside them. `clear` fixes that — it says "don't sit beside a float; start below it":

```css
.footer {
  clear: both;
}
```

## The old way to build columns

Before Flexbox, people built whole page layouts by floating boxes side by side:

```css
.col {
  float: left;
  width: 33.33%;
}
```

You'll see this in older websites and templates. It works, but it's fiddly (you constantly have to clear floats). **Don't build new layouts this way** — Flexbox and Grid, which you'll learn next, do the same job far more easily.

## The takeaway

- **Do** use `float` to wrap text around an image.
- **Don't** use it to build page columns — reach for Flexbox or Grid instead.
- **Recognise** it in older code so it doesn't confuse you.

**Try it:** in `style.css`, `float: left` an image and give it a `margin-right`, then write a paragraph after it and watch the text wrap around it.

## Where you will see this happen

1. Save both files with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R**.
2. The image should sit on the left with the paragraph text running up beside it and carrying on underneath it.
3. If the text sits below the image instead, there is not enough of it. The wrap only shows when the text is long enough to run past the image — paste in a few more sentences and reload.
4. The words should not touch the image. If they do, the `margin-right` is missing.
5. The paragraph must come **after** the image in your HTML. Text written before a floated image never wraps around it.
6. After every edit: save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R**.

## Recap — the short version

- Float only looks as though it worked when there is enough text after the image — with one short line the text drops below and it appears that nothing happened.
- The content that wraps has to come **after** the floated element in the HTML.
- Give a `float: left` image a `margin-right`, or the words will run right up against it.
- A floated element leaves the normal flow, so its container can collapse to nothing; `clear: both` on a later element makes it start below the float.
- Use float to wrap text around an image. Do not build page columns with it — Flexbox and Grid do that job, and they are coming up next.

courses.title: Overflow and z-index
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to wrap text around an image with `float` and push later content below it with `clear`

Sometimes content is bigger than the box meant to hold it — a long paragraph in a fixed-height card, a wide table on a phone. **`overflow`** decides what happens to the part that doesn't fit. And **`z-index`** decides what sits on top when things overlap.

## overflow

When content spills out of a box with a set size, `overflow` controls it:

```css
.box {
  height: 150px;
  overflow: auto;     /* add a scrollbar only if needed */
}
```

The values:
- `visible` — the default; content spills out and is still shown.
- `hidden` — clip off (hide) anything that doesn't fit.
- `scroll` — always show scrollbars.
- `auto` — show scrollbars **only when needed** (usually what you want).

A common real use: `overflow-x: auto` on a wide table's wrapper so it scrolls sideways on small screens instead of breaking the page:

```css
.table-wrap {
  overflow-x: auto;
}
```

## z-index — the stacking order

When elements overlap (usually because of positioning), `z-index` decides which one is in front. Higher numbers sit on top:

```css
.navbar {
  position: fixed;
  z-index: 100;      /* stays above the page content */
}
.modal {
  position: fixed;
  z-index: 1000;     /* above everything, even the navbar */
}
```

Two things to remember:
- `z-index` only works on **positioned** elements (`relative`, `absolute`, `fixed`, or `sticky`) — not on plain static ones.
- Think in "layers": page content low, sticky header higher, pop-ups highest.

**Try it:** in `style.css`, give a fixed-height box some content and `overflow: auto` to get a scrollbar, and give a positioned element a `z-index` so it sits on top of another.

## Where you will see this happen

1. Save `style.css` with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R**.
2. The box with `overflow: auto` should have its own small scrollbar down its right-hand edge. Put the mouse pointer inside the box and scroll: the box scrolls, the page stays still.
3. No scrollbar means the content fits. `auto` shows one only when it is needed, so give the box a set `height` and more text than fits, then reload.
4. For `z-index`, the element you raised should now cover the other one where the two overlap.
5. If neither moved in front, check that element also has a `position` of `relative`, `absolute`, `fixed` or `sticky`.
6. After every edit: save with **Ctrl + S**, click back, press **Ctrl + R**.

## Recap — the short version

- `z-index` does nothing on a static element — it only works once the element also has `position: relative`, `absolute`, `fixed` or `sticky`.
- `overflow: auto` shows a scrollbar only when the content does not fit, so nothing changes until the box has a set `height` and more inside it than fits.
- The four values are `visible` (the default, content spills out), `hidden` (clipped off), `scroll` (always shown) and `auto` (shown when needed).
- `overflow: hidden` really does hide content, which is a common reason text vanishes with no warning.
- `overflow-x: auto` on a wrapper around a wide table lets it scroll sideways on a phone instead of breaking the page.

You'll recognise this pattern on every site you visit from now on. **Try it:** build a `.navbar` with three links: lay them in a row with `display: flex` and `gap`, remove the underline with `text-decoration: none`, and add a `:hover` background. ## Where you will see this happen 1. Until you hover, the `:hover` rule looks as though it did nothing. 4. If the links are stacked down the page, `display: flex` is on the wrong element. courses.title: Flex items and wrapping
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to put `display: flex` on a container so its children sit in a row

You've met Flexbox: `display: flex` on a container lays its children in a row and gives you `justify-content` and `align-items` to position them. This lesson covers controlling the **items** themselves, and making a flex layout **wrap** on small screens.

Start with a container:

```css
.row {
  display: flex;
  gap: 16px;
}
```

## Let items grow and shrink

`flex: 1` on an item tells it to grow and share the available space equally. Put it on several items and they split the row evenly:

```css
.row .box {
  flex: 1;      /* each box takes an equal share of the row */
}
```

Give one item a bigger number to take a bigger share:

```css
.sidebar { flex: 1; }
.main    { flex: 3; }   /* main is 3x as wide as the sidebar */
```

This is how you build a "sidebar + main content" split in two lines.

## Wrapping on small screens

By default flex items stay on one line and squash. `flex-wrap: wrap` lets them drop onto the next line when there isn't room — the key to a card grid that reflows on a phone:

```css
.cards {
  display: flex;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
  gap: 16px;
}
.cards .card {
  flex: 1 1 250px;    /* grow, shrink, but aim for ~250px each */
}
```

`flex: 1 1 250px` means "each card wants to be about 250px; fit as many per row as possible, then wrap." Resize the window and the cards rearrange themselves — responsive with almost no effort.

## Reordering

`order` changes the visual order without touching the HTML:

```css
.featured { order: -1; }   /* jump to the front */
```

## The mental model

- Container: `display: flex`, `gap`, `justify-content`, `align-items`, `flex-wrap`.
- Items: `flex` (grow/share), `order`.

**Try it:** make a `.cards` container `display: flex` with `flex-wrap: wrap` and `gap`, and give each `.card` `flex: 1 1 250px`. Resize the window and watch them wrap.

## Where you will see this happen

Wrapping shows nothing until the browser window is a different width, so you have to change it by hand.

1. If the window fills the whole screen, make it smaller first: **double-click** the bar at the very top of the browser window.
2. Rest the mouse pointer on the **right-hand edge** of the window until it turns into a double-headed arrow.
3. Press and hold the left mouse button, then **drag that edge to the left**, keeping hold as the window narrows.
4. Watch the cards: when there is no longer room for them all, the last one drops onto a new line. Drag back to the right and they return to one line.
5. After any CSS change: save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R**.

## Recap — the short version

- The container takes `display: flex`, `gap` and `flex-wrap`; each item takes `flex` and `order`. Putting `flex-wrap` on an item does nothing at all.
- `flex: 1` on several items splits the row equally. `flex: 3` beside `flex: 1` takes three times the share.
- `flex: 1 1 250px` reads as grow, shrink, aim for about 250px — that third value is what makes cards wrap onto the next line.
- By default flex items squash rather than wrap. Nothing drops onto a new line until you add `flex-wrap: wrap`.
- `order: -1` moves an item to the front on screen without touching the HTML.

courses.title: Layout with Grid
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to line items up in a row with `display: flex` and space them with `gap`

**CSS Grid** is the most powerful layout tool in CSS. Where Flexbox lays things in a single row or column, Grid lays them out in **rows AND columns at the same time** — a true two-dimensional grid. It's perfect for page layouts and image galleries.

**Look at a real one:** any photo gallery or dashboard with a neat grid of equal boxes is almost certainly CSS Grid.

## Turn on Grid

Set `display: grid` on a container and describe the columns you want with `grid-template-columns`:

```css
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr;   /* three equal columns */
  gap: 16px;
}
```

The new unit `fr` means "a fraction of the free space." `1fr 1fr 1fr` = three equal columns. `2fr 1fr` = a wide column and a narrow one.

Every child of `.gallery` now drops neatly into the grid, filling row by row — no floats, no maths.

## The magic responsive line

This one line makes a grid that automatically fits as many columns as will comfortably fit, and reflows on smaller screens:

```css
.gallery {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr));
  gap: 16px;
}
```

Read it as: "make as many columns as fit, each at least 200px wide, sharing space equally." Resize the window and the number of columns changes on its own. This is the go-to recipe for responsive card grids and galleries.

## Rows and gaps

- `gap: 16px` — space between every row and column (works in Flexbox too).
- `grid-template-rows: 100px auto` — set explicit row heights if you need them.

## Grid vs Flexbox — which?

- **One direction** (a row of nav links, a toolbar) → Flexbox.
- **Two directions / a real grid** (galleries, page layouts, dashboards) → Grid.

They work beautifully together: Grid for the page skeleton, Flexbox inside each area.

**Try it:** make a `.gallery` `display: grid` with `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` and a `gap`, then put several boxes inside and resize the window.

## Recap — the short version

- `display: grid` and `grid-template-columns` go on the CONTAINER. The children need no rule of their own — they drop into the grid in order.
- `fr` means one share of the leftover space, so `1fr 1fr 1fr` is three equal columns and `2fr 1fr` is a wide one beside a narrow one.
- `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` is the line worth memorising: as many columns as fit, each at least 200px, sharing the space evenly.
- One direction, such as a row of nav links, calls for Flexbox. Two directions, such as a gallery or a page skeleton, calls for Grid.
- `gap` sets the space between rows and columns, and works in Flexbox as well.

courses.title: Pseudo-classes & pseudo-elements
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write a CSS rule that targets a class such as `.card`

**Pseudo-classes** and **pseudo-elements** let you style elements in special *states* (like being hovered) or style *parts* of an element you didn't write into the HTML. They power a huge amount of interactive, polished design.

## Pseudo-classes — style a state

A pseudo-class starts with a single colon `:` and targets an element when it's in a certain state.

`:hover` — while the mouse is over it (you've seen this):

```css
button:hover {
  background-color: #444;
}
```

`:focus` — while it's selected (an input being typed in, a link tabbed to). Important for accessibility:

```css
input:focus {
  outline: 2px solid dodgerblue;
}
```

`:active` — while it's being clicked. `:first-child` / `:last-child` — the first or last child of its parent:

```css
li:last-child {
  border-bottom: none;   /* no divider under the final item */
}
```

`:nth-child(even)` — every even item, great for striped table rows:

```css
tr:nth-child(even) {
  background-color: #f4f4f4;
}
```

## Pseudo-elements — style a part

A pseudo-element starts with a **double** colon `::` and styles a piece of an element.

`::first-line`, `::first-letter` style exactly what they say. The big two are `::before` and `::after`, which insert generated content:

```css
.price::before {
  content: "$";      /* adds a $ in front of every price */
}
.badge::after {
  content: " ★";
}
```

`::before` and `::after` always need a `content` property (even if empty: `content: ""`). They're used everywhere for decorative touches, icons, and shapes.

## Remember the colons

- **One colon** `:` = a *state* (`:hover`, `:focus`, `:nth-child`).
- **Two colons** `::` = a *part* (`::before`, `::after`, `::first-letter`).

**Try it:** in `style.css`, add a `:hover` effect to a button, an `:focus` outline to an input, and use `::after` with `content` to append a symbol to an element.

## Where you will see this happen

`:hover` and `:focus` show nothing on a page that is just sitting there. You have to move the mouse or click into a box.

1. Move the mouse pointer on top of your button and hold it still — do not click. The background colour changes while the pointer is over it, and changes back when you move away.
2. Click once inside your `<input>` box so a text cursor blinks in it. The `:focus` outline appears around the box.
3. Click an empty part of the page. The outline disappears.
4. Look at the element you gave `::after` — its symbol is there from the moment the page loads, no mouse needed.

After every CSS change: save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R**.

## Recap — the short version

- One colon is a state — `:hover`, `:focus`, `:active`, `:nth-child`. Two colons is a part of an element — `::before`, `::after`, `::first-letter`.
- `::before` and `::after` show nothing without a `content` property, even when it is empty: `content: "";`
- There is no space before the colon. `button:hover` means the button while hovered; `button :hover` means something else entirely.
- `:nth-child(even)` striping table rows and `:last-child` removing the final divider are the two you will reach for most.
- `:focus` is what keyboard users rely on to see where they are, so never remove an outline without putting a visible one back.

courses.title: Transitions
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to write a `:hover` rule that changes an element's colour

A **transition** makes a change happen *smoothly* over time instead of instantly. It's the single easiest way to make a page feel polished — a button that eases into its hover colour feels far nicer than one that snaps.

## The problem

By default, a `:hover` change is instant:

```css
.btn {
  background-color: #6a11cb;
}
.btn:hover {
  background-color: #2575fc;   /* snaps immediately */
}
```

## The fix: one line

Add a `transition` to the element telling it which property to animate and how long to take:

```css
.btn {
  background-color: #6a11cb;
  transition: background-color 0.3s ease;
}
.btn:hover {
  background-color: #2575fc;   /* now fades over 0.3s */
}
```

Now the colour eases in over 0.3 seconds. That's the whole trick — put `transition` on the **normal** state, and any change (from `:hover`, `:focus`, or JavaScript) animates automatically.

## Transitioning several things

Use `all` to animate every change, or list several:

```css
.card {
  transition: transform 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease;
}
.card:hover {
  transform: translateY(-4px);          /* lifts up */
  box-shadow: 0 8px 20px rgba(0,0,0,0.15);
}
```

That's the "card lifts and its shadow grows on hover" effect you see everywhere — and now you can build it.

## The pieces

`transition: <property> <duration> <timing>;`
- **property** — what to animate (`background-color`, `transform`, or `all`).
- **duration** — how long (`0.3s`, `200ms`).
- **timing** — the easing curve (`ease` is a good default; also `linear`, `ease-in-out`).

## Keep it quick

Good transitions are fast — `0.15s` to `0.3s`. Anything slower than about half a second starts to feel sluggish.

**Try it:** in `style.css`, add `transition: all 0.2s ease` to a button or card, then give it a `:hover` that changes the background and lifts it with `transform: translateY(-4px)`.

## Where you will see this happen

A transition lasts a fraction of a second, so it is easy to look straight past it.

1. Save `style.css` with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.
2. Move the mouse pointer onto the button and hold it still. The new colour should **fade** in over about a third of a second rather than appearing at once.
3. Move the pointer away without clicking. The old colour fades back the same way.
4. Not sure it is working? Delete the `transition` line, save, reload, and hover again — now the colour snaps instantly. Put the line back, save and reload.
5. Try changing `0.3s` to `2s` to make the fade impossible to miss, then set it back.

After every change: save with **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R**.

## Recap — the short version

- `transition` goes on the NORMAL rule, not inside the `:hover` rule. Written on the element itself, it smooths every change in both directions.
- The shape is `transition: <property> <duration> <timing>`, for example `transition: background-color 0.3s ease`.
- `all` animates every property that changes. To name several instead, separate them with commas: `transform 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease`.
- Durations of `0.15s` to `0.3s` feel right. Anything past half a second starts to feel sluggish.
- A transition can only smooth a change that something else causes — a `:hover`, a `:focus`, or JavaScript later on.

courses.title: CSS units: px, rem, %, vh
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to set sizes such as `padding` and `width` in pixels

CSS sizes can be written in several **units**. Choosing the right one is the difference between a layout that adapts nicely and one that breaks. Here are the ones that matter.

## px — absolute pixels

A fixed size that never changes:

```css
border: 1px solid black;
font-size: 16px;
```

Great for things that should stay exact — borders, small fixed spacing. But a whole layout built in `px` can't adapt, so we mix in relative units too.

## % — percentage of the parent

Relative to the containing element:

```css
.col {
  width: 50%;   /* half of its parent's width */
}
```

Perfect for widths that should flex with the screen.

## em and rem — relative to font size

- `rem` is relative to the **root** font size (usually 16px). `1rem` = 16px, `2rem` = 32px. Predictable and the modern favourite for spacing and type.
- `em` is relative to the **current element's** font size. Handy inside components, but it compounds (nesting multiplies it), so it can surprise you.

```css
h1 { font-size: 2rem; }     /* 32px */
p  { font-size: 1rem; }     /* 16px */
.card { padding: 1.5rem; }  /* 24px */
```

Using `rem` means if you ever change the base font size, the whole page scales together.

## vw and vh — relative to the screen

`vw` = 1% of the viewport width, `vh` = 1% of the viewport height. Great for full-screen sections:

```css
.hero {
  height: 100vh;    /* exactly one screen tall */
}
```

## A simple rule of thumb

- **Borders, small fixed details** → `px`.
- **Font sizes and spacing** → `rem`.
- **Widths that should flex** → `%` (or `fr` in Grid).
- **Full-screen sections** → `vh` / `vw`.

Mixing units on purpose is how responsive pages are built.

**Try it:** in `style.css`, set a heading's `font-size` in `rem`, a column's `width` in `%`, and a hero section's `height` to `100vh`.

## Recap — the short version

- `rem` is measured from the root font size, usually 16px, so `2rem` is 32px wherever you write it. `em` is measured from the element's own font size, and nesting multiplies it.
- There is never a space between the number and the unit: `16px`, not `16 px`. A plain `0` needs no unit.
- `%` is a share of the parent element, while `vw` and `vh` are a share of the screen — `height: 100vh` is exactly one screenful tall.
- Rule of thumb: `px` for borders and small fixed details, `rem` for type and spacing, `%` or `fr` for widths that should flex, `vh` for full-screen sections.
- A layout built entirely in `px` cannot adapt. Mixing units on purpose is what makes a page responsive.

courses.title: Specificity & the cascade
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to select elements by tag name, class and id in `style.css` Sooner or later two CSS rules will try to style the same thing in different ways. Which one wins? The answer is **specificity** and the **cascade** — and understanding it ends the "why won't my CSS change?" frustration for good. ## The cascade: later wins (all else equal) If two rules have the *same* specificity, the one written **later** in the file wins: ```css p { color: blue; } p { color: red; } /* wins — it comes later. Text is red. */ ``` ## Specificity: more specific wins But a *more specific* selector beats a later one. Roughly, from weakest to strongest: 1. **Element** selectors (`p`, `h1`) — weakest. 2. **Class** selectors (`.intro`, `:hover`) — stronger. 3. **ID** selectors (`#header`) — stronger still. 4. **Inline** `style="..."` — strongest of the normal ones. ```css p { color: blue; } .intro { color: green; } /* a class beats an element */ #lead { color: red; } /* an id beats a class */ ``` A `

` ends up **red**, because the id wins — even though the element rule came... wherever. ## Inheritance Some properties (like `color` and `font-family`) are **inherited** — set them on `body` and children get them for free unless they override: ```css body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; color: #333; } /* every element inside now uses these, unless it says otherwise */ ``` ## !important — the emergency brake (avoid) Adding `!important` forces a declaration to win over everything: ```css p { color: blue !important; } ``` It works, but it's a sledgehammer — it overrides specificity and is hard to undo later. **Avoid it.** If you're reaching for `!important`, it usually means a selector needs to be more specific instead. ## The practical takeaway If a style "won't apply," another rule is probably beating it. Check: is something more specific (an id, a class) overriding your element selector? Make your selector match, rather than piling on `!important`. **Try it:** in `style.css`, style a `p` one colour, then a `.special` class another, and see the class win on a `

`. Set `color` on `body` and watch it inherit. ## Recap — the short version - The rule of thumb: an id beats a class, and a class beats a plain tag name. When two rules are of equal strength, the one written further down the file wins. - If a style "will not apply", it is almost never broken — something more specific is beating it. Find that rule instead of guessing. - The fix is to make your selector match the winning one, not to pile on `!important`, which overrides everything and is painful to undo later. - `color` and `font-family` are inherited: set them on `body` and everything inside gets them unless it says otherwise. - An inline `style="..."` attribute in the HTML beats all your normal rules in `style.css`, which is one good reason to avoid it.

courses.title: Git and GitHub
courses.description:
> **Before this lesson,** you should be able to move between folders in the terminal with `pwd`, `ls` and `cd`

These two words sound very technical, but the ideas behind them are simple. Let us take them one at a time, slowly.

## What is Git?

**Git** is a tool on your computer that **saves the history of your work**. Each time you finish a little bit, you tell Git to save a snapshot — this snapshot is called a **commit**. If you ever make a mess, your snapshots are still there to go back to. You already installed Git in an earlier lesson (it came bundled with Git Bash).

## What is GitHub?

**GitHub** is a **website** that keeps a copy of your project online. A simple way to picture it:

- **Git** is like the *Save* button on your own computer.
- **GitHub** is like the *cloud* where your saves are backed up and shared.

On LaceFi Academy, GitHub is also the place where a robot checks your work and tells you if it passed.

## What to do

Follow these steps in order. If you are new to Git and GitHub, don't worry — each step is explained below.

### 1. Accept the assignment and download your repository

First, accept the assignment. You will then get your own private GitHub repository.

Copy the repository URL and open your terminal (**Git Bash** on Windows, **Terminal** on a Mac).

Run:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_URL
```

For example:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/your-username/my-assignment.git
```

Then move into the project folder:

```bash
cd my-assignment
```

You now have a copy of the assignment on your computer that you can work on.

### 2. Work on the assignment and save your progress

Open the project folder in your code editor, such as VS Code.

Edit the files and complete the assignment.

When you want to save your progress to GitHub, run these commands:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "My work"
git push
```

Here's what they do:

* `git add .` — tells Git which changes you want to save.
* `git commit -m "My work"` — creates a saved version of your work.
* `git push` — uploads your saved work to GitHub.

**You can push as many times as you want. Pushing does not submit or grade your assignment.**

### 3. Submit your assignment for grading

When you have finished and are ready for the robot to check your work, create a submission tag:

```bash
git tag submit/1
```

Then send the tag to GitHub:

```bash
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the grading system:

> "I am ready. Please check my assignment."

The automated grader will run and check your work against the assignment requirements.

### 4. Check your results and fix any problems

After grading finishes, open your assignment results and check which requirements passed and which ones failed.

* ✅ **Check** means that requirement passed.
* ❌ **Cross** means that requirement needs to be fixed.

If something fails, go back to your code and fix it.

Save and push your changes again:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Fix assignment"
git push
```

Then submit a new version:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

If you need to make more fixes, repeat the process using `submit/3`, `submit/4`, and so on.

**Remember:** normal `git push` saves your work. A `submit/N` tag is what sends your work for grading.

## Where you will see this happen

After you push a `submit/` tag, the checking happens on GitHub, not on your computer. Nothing appears on your screen, so you have to go and look.

1. Open your web browser and go to your assignment repository on `https://github.com`.
2. Click the **Actions** tab near the top of the repository page.
3. The newest run sits at the top. A yellow dot means it is still working, a green check means it passed, a red cross means something failed.
4. Click the run, then the job inside it, to read each requirement line by line.

A run takes a minute or two, so if the page still looks empty, press **Ctrl + R** *(Mac: **Command + R**)* to reload it and look again.

## Recap — the short version

- `git push` saves your work online and grades nothing. Only a `submit/N` tag asks the robot to check it.
- The three saving commands always go in the same order: `git add .`, then `git commit -m "My work"`, then `git push`.
- You clone a repository once with `git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_URL`, then `cd` into the folder it makes before you touch anything.
- Each new submission needs the next number — `submit/2`, `submit/3` — because a tag name can be used only once.
- Git is the save button on your own computer; GitHub is the website that keeps a copy online.
